case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a party may move under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(b)(4) to vacate a default judgment that is void for lack of personal jurisdiction at any time, or whether Rule 60(c)(1) requires the motion to be filed within a "reasonable time."
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(b)(4) (relief from a void judgment) and Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(c)(1) (timing: "A motion under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time").
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Coney Island argues that because a judgment entered without personal jurisdiction is void ab initio, Rule 60(b)(4) relief is mandatory and cannot be constrained by any timeliness limitation; therefore Rule 60(c)(1)'s "reasonable time" requirement should not apply (or should not operate as a time bar) to motions challenging void judgments for lack of personal jurisdiction, even when brought long after entry of the default.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The Trustee argues the text of Rule 60(c)(1) is categorical—any motion under Rule 60(b), including 60(b)(4), must be filed within a reasonable time—and this Court’s precedent (including Kemp) confirms that all Rule 60(b) motions are subject to that timing requirement; allowing voidness challenges at any time would undermine finality and, in this case, would destabilize a nearly fully administered Chapter 7 estate and reward delay.
key_precedents: Kemp v. United States (statement that "[a]ll" Rule 60(b) motions must be filed within a reasonable time)
United Student Aid Funds, Inc. v. Espinosa, 559 U.S. 260 (2010)
Link v. Wabash R.R. Co., 370 U.S. 626 (1962)
World Trade Ctr. Disaster Site Litig., 722 F.3d 483 (2d Cir. 2013)
United States for Use & Benefit of Mosher Steel Co. v. Fluor Corp., 436 F.2d 383 (2d Cir. 1970)
Allstate Life Ins. Co. v. Linter Grp. Ltd., 994 F.2d 996 (2d Cir. 1993)
Zervos v. Verizon N.Y., Inc., 252 F.3d 163 (2d Cir. 2001)
United States v. Boch Oldsmobile, Inc., 909 F.2d 657 (1st Cir. 1990)

John Roberts.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains the traditional maxim that a void judgment is a nullity and so may be attacked at any time, particularly for want of personal jurisdiction; but Rule 60(c)(1) is categorical that a motion “under Rule 60(b)” must be made within a reasonable time, and I agree with Justice Alito that the Rules’ structure—especially the explicit one-year cap for 60(b)(1)–(3)—shows the drafters knew how to specify distinct timing regimes and chose not to exempt (b)(4). Justice Kagan’s reliance on Kemp strengthens the textual conclusion because Kemp describes the reasonable-time requirement as applying to “all” Rule 60(b) motions, which makes an atextual carveout for (b)(4) difficult to justify. Espinosa, as Justice Sotomayor emphasizes, further supports a narrow, finality-respecting approach by rejecting (b)(4) as a license to sleep on rights; we can resolve this case on timeliness grounds while leaving the outer bounds of “voidness” largely untouched.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains the maxim that a void judgment is a nullity subject to attack at any time, particularly for want of personal jurisdiction. But Rule 60(c)(1) is enacted text, and it states categorically that a motion “under Rule 60(b)” must be made within a reasonable time; a (b)(4) motion is still “under Rule 60(b),” so courts have no warrant to invent an atextual exemption. Justice Alito’s structural point—that the Rules expressly created a different timing regime for (b)(1)–(3) but not for (b)(4)—confirms the ordinary textual reading, and Kemp’s statement (noted by the Chief Justice) that “all” Rule 60(b) motions are subject to the reasonable-time requirement reinforces that conclusion. Espinosa further undercuts petitioner’s absolutist premise by insisting (b)(4) relief is exceptional and not a license to sleep on rights, which fits comfortably within a reasonableness inquiry that can be generous when notice truly was lacking.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point—the traditional maxim that a void judgment is a nullity subject to attack at any time—cannot override the enacted text of Rule 60(c)(1), which categorically requires that any motion “under Rule 60(b)” be brought within a reasonable time, with no carveout for (b)(4). Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Kemp is particularly persuasive because it describes the reasonable-time requirement as applying to “all” Rule 60(b) motions, and the Rule’s separate one-year limit for (b)(1)–(3) confirms, as Justice Barrett notes, that the drafters knew how to write explicit timing distinctions when intended. Espinosa, highlighted by Justice Kagan, further undercuts the “any time” theory by emphasizing that (b)(4) is narrow and not a license to sleep on rights—finality remains a substantial value even in jurisdictional disputes. A flexible reasonableness inquiry adequately protects genuine lack-of-notice cases while preventing disruptive, strategic, long-delayed collateral attacks that would destabilize reliance interests, especially in bankruptcy administration.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point—the due-process maxim that a truly void judgment can be attacked “at any time”—has force where a party lacked notice or personal jurisdiction, but it cannot override Rule 60(c)(1)’s unqualified command that any motion “under Rule 60(b)” be made within a reasonable time. As Justice Kagan emphasizes, a (b)(4) request is still a Rule 60(b) motion, and Kemp’s language—highlighted by Chief Justice Roberts—that the reasonable-time requirement applies to “all” Rule 60(b) motions makes an atextual carveout especially hard to justify. Espinosa’s warning, which Justice Jackson and the Chief also stress, answers the equity concern from the other direction: (b)(4) is not a license to sleep on rights, and a generous, fact-sensitive “reasonable time” inquiry can protect blameless parties while respecting reliance interests (particularly in a nearly administered bankruptcy estate). I therefore would affirm on timeliness while leaving the outer bounds of “voidness” largely for another day, rather than constitutionalizing an unlimited reopening rule that could harm third parties and destabilize settled distributions.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point—the common-law maxim that a void judgment can be attacked “at any time,” especially for lack of personal jurisdiction—has force as a background principle, but it cannot displace Rule 60(c)(1)’s enacted text requiring that any motion “under Rule 60(b)” be brought within a reasonable time. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito emphasize, Kemp’s statement that the reasonable-time requirement applies to “all” Rule 60(b) motions and the Rules’ express one-year limit for (b)(1)–(3) make an implied (b)(4) carveout textually untenable. Espinosa, highlighted by Justice Sotomayor, reinforces that (b)(4) is not a license to sleep on rights—supporting a pragmatic, flexible reasonableness inquiry that can be generous where notice was truly lacking yet still protects reliance interests and finality. No colleague has offered a precedent or structural argument that meaningfully weakens the straightforward reading that (b)(4) remains subject to Rule 60(c)(1).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest argument—the common-law maxim that a void judgment may be attacked at any time—cannot displace the enacted text of Rule 60(c)(1), which states without exception that a motion “under Rule 60(b)” must be made within a reasonable time, and Rule 60(b)(4) is plainly within that category. Chief Justice Roberts’s point is persuasive that the “reasonable time” standard can be applied generously when notice truly was absent, protecting due process without inventing an atextual carveout. Justice Alito’s structural observation that the Rules expressly imposed a one-year cap for 60(b)(1)–(3) but did not exempt (b)(4) confirms we should not judicially add an “any time” rule, and Kemp/Espinosa reinforce that timeliness and finality remain integral constraints even for (b)(4). Nothing raised in conference undermines the textualist reading; at most it argues for a permissive application of “reasonable time,” not its elimination.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest argument—the historic maxim that a void judgment can be attacked “at any time,” particularly for lack of personal jurisdiction—cannot displace the enacted text of Rule 60(c)(1), which states categorically that a motion “under Rule 60(b)” must be made within a reasonable time and contains no (b)(4) carveout. Chief Justice Roberts’s institutional, minimalist approach is persuasive: enforcing timeliness preserves finality and reliance interests (especially in bankruptcy) while still allowing courts to treat “reasonable time” generously when the movant truly lacked notice, so due process is not diluted. Justice Alito’s structural point that the Rules expressly created different timing regimes (the one-year bar for 60(b)(1)–(3)) underscores that an “any time” exception for (b)(4) would be atextual. Kemp’s statement that “all” Rule 60(b) motions are subject to Rule 60(c)(1), together with Espinosa’s warning that (b)(4) is not a license to sleep on rights, reinforces that timeliness is part of the Rule’s framework even for voidness claims.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument remains the common-law maxim that a void judgment may be attacked at any time, particularly for want of personal jurisdiction, but that maxim cannot displace the enacted text of Rule 60(c)(1), which provides without exception that a motion “under Rule 60(b)” must be brought within a reasonable time. Justice Alito’s structural point is decisive under a textualist methodology: the Rules expressly impose a one-year limit for (b)(1)–(3) yet do not create an “any time” exemption for (b)(4), indicating courts may not engraft one. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Kemp and Espinosa reinforces that “reasonable time” applies to all Rule 60(b) motions and that (b)(4) is not a license to sleep on rights, while still allowing reasonableness to be sensitive to genuine notice and due-process defects. No colleague identified contrary precedent or text that genuinely undermines this reading, so I would affirm on timeliness without expanding the concept of voidness beyond our cases.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point—the common-law maxim that a void judgment may be attacked “at any time,” especially for want of personal jurisdiction—carries serious due-process force, but it cannot override Rule 60(c)(1)’s categorical command that a motion “under Rule 60(b)” be made within a reasonable time. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Kemp is persuasive because it treats the reasonable-time requirement as applying to “all” Rule 60(b) motions, undercutting any judge-made carveout for (b)(4), while Espinosa (as Justice Sotomayor stresses) rejects using (b)(4) as a license to “sleep on rights.” On a pragmatic, procedural-fairness view, the right answer is not an unlimited reopening rule but a reasonableness standard that is highly sensitive to lack of notice and blameless delay, yet still protects reliance interests—especially in a nearly administered bankruptcy estate. Nothing in the text or structure (including the drafters’ explicit one-year limit for (b)(1)–(3), as Justice Alito notes) supports converting (b)(4) into an at-any-time collateral-attack mechanism.

John Roberts.reasoning: Rule 60(c)(1) states categorically that "[a] motion under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time," and the Court in Kemp read that timing command to apply to all Rule 60(b) motions, which counsels against carving out an atextual exception for Rule 60(b)(4). Espinosa likewise emphasizes that Rule 60(b)(4) relief is reserved for the exceptional case where the rendering court lacked even an arguable basis for jurisdiction, reflecting the Court’s insistence on finality and limited collateral attack rather than an open-ended invitation to relitigate long-settled judgments. A narrow ruling enforcing the reasonable-time requirement—while recognizing that what is "reasonable" may be generous when a judgment truly is void for want of personal jurisdiction—best reconciles the Rules’ text with institutional interests in finality, especially in a nearly administered bankruptcy estate. On that approach, the motion may be denied as untimely without deciding more than necessary about the outer boundaries of voidness doctrine.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Rules’ text is controlling: Rule 60(c)(1) provides without exception that “[a] motion under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time,” and a motion under Rule 60(b)(4) is plainly a “motion under Rule 60(b).” While a judgment entered without personal jurisdiction is void, Espinosa confirms Rule 60(b)(4) relief is reserved for the “exceptional case” where the rendering court lacked even an arguable basis for jurisdiction, and nothing in the Rules’ text creates a categorical “any time” carveout for (b)(4). Kemp likewise underscores that all Rule 60(b) motions are subject to Rule 60(c)(1)’s timing requirement, and finality concerns reinforce adhering to the Rule as written rather than engrafting an extra-textual exception.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of Rule 60(c)(1) is categorical: “A motion under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time,” and it contains no carveout for Rule 60(b)(4) motions alleging lack of personal jurisdiction. This Court’s decision in Kemp confirms the ordinary reading—“All” Rule 60(b) motions are subject to the “reasonable time” requirement—while the Rule’s separate one-year cap for 60(b)(1)–(3) shows the drafters knew how to create special timing rules and chose not to do so for (b)(4). Allowing a voidness challenge at any time would undermine finality and create serious practical disruption, particularly in contexts like a nearly fully administered bankruptcy estate, and Espinosa reinforces that Rule 60(b)(4) is not a boundless vehicle for reopening judgments long after the fact. Accordingly, a court may deny a 60(b)(4) motion as untimely when it is not brought within a reasonable time under Rule 60(c)(1).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Rule 60(c)(1) states categorically that “[a] motion under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time,” and Kemp v. United States reinforces that “all” Rule 60(b) motions are subject to that timing constraint, including those under Rule 60(b)(4). Espinosa further cautions that Rule 60(b)(4) “does not provide a license for litigants to sleep on their rights,” recognizing forfeiture where a party with actual notice fails to raise a timely objection—an approach that respects due process while preventing strategic delay. A reasonable-time inquiry is pragmatic and equitable: it can account for when the movant learned of the judgment and the prejudice to others who relied on finality, which is especially acute in a nearly fully administered Chapter 7 estate. Preserving access to justice for vulnerable parties does not require endorsing open-ended collateral attacks that would destabilize settled distributions where the movant had notice and delayed without justification.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Rule 60(c)(1) states categorically that “[a] motion under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time,” and Rule 60(b)(4) is a motion “under Rule 60(b),” so the timing requirement applies by its terms. Kemp reinforces that understanding by describing the reasonable-time limit as governing “all” Rule 60(b) motions, and Espinosa likewise emphasizes that Rule 60(b)(4) is not “a license for litigants to sleep on their rights,” recognizing forfeiture through inaction and the centrality of finality. A “reasonable time” standard remains workable and calibrated: it preserves relief for truly void judgments (including for want of personal jurisdiction) while allowing courts to account for notice, diligence, and prejudice—particularly salient where reopening a default judgment would disrupt a nearly administered bankruptcy estate.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The text of Rule 60(c)(1) is categorical: “A motion under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time,” and Rule 60(b)(4) is plainly “under Rule 60(b),” so courts may enforce a reasonable-time requirement even when voidness is alleged. This Court has underscored that Rule 60(b)(4) is narrow, reserving relief for exceptional cases where the rendering court lacked even an arguable basis for jurisdiction, reflecting the Rules’ concern for finality. See United Student Aid Funds, Inc. v. Espinosa, 559 U.S. 260, 271 (2010). And Kemp’s statement that “all” Rule 60(b) motions are subject to Rule 60(c)(1)’s timing requirement reinforces the ordinary meaning of the Rules’ structure and counsels against judicially creating an atextual exemption for 60(b)(4).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Rule 60(c)(1) states categorically that “[a] motion under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time,” and Rule 60(b)(4) is not textually exempt from that timing rule. This Court’s understanding in Kemp confirms that “all” Rule 60(b) motions are subject to Rule 60(c)(1)’s reasonable-time requirement, and Espinosa further cautions that Rule 60(b)(4) relief is reserved for the exceptional case where the rendering court lacked even an arguable basis for jurisdiction—reflecting strong finality concerns. Consistent with precedent, history, and practical workability (especially in bankruptcy administration), the better reading is that voidness is a narrow merits inquiry and the motion still must be brought within a reasonable time, with “reasonable” calibrated to protect due process while preventing strategic delay.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of Rule 60(c)(1) is categorical: “A motion under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time,” and Rule 60(b)(4) is undisputedly “under Rule 60(b),” so the ordinary textual reading applies. Kemp confirms that “all” Rule 60(b) motions are subject to Rule 60(c)(1)’s timing requirement, and nothing in the Rules carves out voidness challenges from that command. Espinosa likewise treats Rule 60(b)(4) relief as reserved for exceptional cases of truly jurisdictionless judgments, which is consistent with enforcing the Rule’s procedural limits to protect finality—especially where the movant had notice and delayed while reliance interests accrued. Accordingly, a 60(b)(4) movant may challenge a judgment entered without personal jurisdiction, but must do so within a “reasonable time” as Rule 60(c)(1) requires.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Rule 60(c)(1) states categorically that “[a] motion under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time,” and that text naturally includes motions under Rule 60(b)(4). While a judgment entered without personal jurisdiction violates due process and is “void,” Espinosa teaches that Rule 60(b)(4) relief is reserved for the exceptional case where the rendering court lacked even an arguable basis for jurisdiction, and it reflects a concern for finality even in voidness challenges. Reading Rule 60(c)(1) as inapplicable would invite strategic delay and disrupt reliance interests—concerns especially acute in a nearly fully administered Chapter 7 estate—while still allowing courts, in assessing “reasonable time,” to account for notice and fairness to the defaulted party. Kemp’s statement that “all” Rule 60(b) motions are subject to the reasonable-time requirement reinforces that a timeliness inquiry applies even when the asserted defect is jurisdictional.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a party may seek relief from a default judgment that is void for lack of personal jurisdiction under Rule 60(b)(4) at any time, or whether Rule 60(c)(1) requires such a motion to be filed within a “reasonable time.”
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(b)(4) (void judgments) and Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(c)(1) (timing: “within a reasonable time” for motions under Rule 60(b)); implicated constitutional principle: Due Process limits on exercising personal jurisdiction.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that because a judgment entered without personal jurisdiction is void ab initio, Rule 60(b)(4) relief is mandatory once voidness is shown and cannot be cut off by Rule 60(c)(1)’s “reasonable time” language; imposing a timeliness bar would improperly allow an unconstitutional/ultra vires judgment to become effectively valid through passage of time, especially in default-judgment settings where the defendant never appeared.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent argues the text of Rule 60(c)(1) is categorical—any motion under Rule 60(b), including (b)(4), must be made within a reasonable time—and the Sixth Circuit correctly enforced that limit to protect finality and prevent disruptive, chaos-inducing late challenges (here, in the context of a nearly fully administered Chapter 7 estate); respondent also cites Supreme Court language (including Kemp) indicating that all Rule 60(b) motions are subject to the “reasonable time” requirement.
key_precedents: Kemp v. United States (statement that all Rule 60(b) motions must be filed within a reasonable time)
United Student Aid Funds, Inc. v. Espinosa, 559 U.S. 260 (2010) (Rule 60(b)(4) and treatment of voidness; cited as suggesting void judgments can be attacked later)
Klapprott v. United States, 335 U.S. 601 (1949) (discussion of Rule 60 and assumption in opinions about lack of a definite time limit for certain relief; referenced in briefing regarding (b)(4))
United States for Use & Benefit of Mosher Steel Co. v. Fluor Corp., 436 F.2d 383 (2d Cir. 1970) (court discretion to refer parties to rendering court; comity in judgment enforcement context)
Allstate Life Ins. Co. v. Linter Group Ltd., 994 F.2d 996 (2d Cir. 1993) (comity/registration court discretion; abuse-of-discretion review)
World Trade Ctr. Disaster Site Litig., 722 F.3d 483 (2d Cir. 2013) (inherent power to manage dockets)
Link v. Wabash R.R. Co., 370 U.S. 626 (1962) (inherent authority to manage cases)
Zervos v. Verizon N.Y., Inc., 252 F.3d 163 (2d Cir. 2001) (abuse-of-discretion formulation referenced in the record)
United States v. Boch Oldsmobile, Inc., 909 F.2d 657 (1st Cir. 1990) (cited as authority on attacking void judgments under Rule 60(b)(4))

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Kagan press the strongest point: Rule 60(c)(1) says motions “under Rule 60(b)” must be made within a reasonable time, and Kemp’s broad language about “all” Rule 60(b) motions cannot be wished away. But that reading, applied to an Espinosa-level void judgment (no even arguable personal jurisdiction or fundamental notice defect), risks turning a timing provision for reopening into a practical authorization to continue enforcing a nullity—something finality cannot supply and the Rules should not be read to accomplish absent clear statement. I agree with Justice Gorsuch that we can respect the text and Espinosa’s “sleep on rights” admonition by treating delay as highly relevant to whether the movant has actually shown true voidness (as opposed to a waivable or merely erroneous defect), while holding that once that exceptional threshold is met, vacatur is mandatory and timeliness alone cannot bar relief. Kemp affects my analysis only to the extent it cautions against an expansive carveout; our holding should therefore be narrow, limited to demonstrated Espinosa-void default judgments, which best preserves institutional legitimacy while avoiding the implication that jurisdiction can be supplied by the passage of time.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is the categorical text of Rule 60(c)(1) applying to all motions “under Rule 60(b),” reinforced by Kemp’s general language; on a purely surface reading, that cuts for respondent. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, that text does not resolve the antecedent question whether a judgment shown to be Espinosa-void—entered without even an arguable basis for personal jurisdiction and thus without lawful adjudicative authority—can be kept on the books and enforced by invoking a timing rule; under the original public meaning of “void,” a nullity cannot acquire legal force through delay. Espinosa’s “no license to sleep on rights” admonition is best read, consistent with its holding, as narrowing the category of voidness (thereby addressing finality) rather than empowering courts to deny relief once true voidness is established. I would therefore accept a narrow approach (as Roberts suggests) allowing delay to inform whether the asserted defect is genuinely Espinosa-level voidness, but not to bar vacatur once that threshold is met.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas press the strongest point: a judgment entered without personal jurisdiction is a due-process nullity, and time cannot “cure” a lack of adjudicative authority. But that framing still does not answer the textual question what Rule 60(c)(1) directs federal courts to do when a party invokes the reopening mechanism: it says motions “under Rule 60(b)”—without exempting (b)(4)—“must be made within a reasonable time,” and, as Justice Kagan notes, that limit governs the availability of extraordinary relief rather than retroactively conferring jurisdiction. Espinosa’s warning that (b)(4) is not a “license … to sleep on their rights,” and Kemp’s broad treatment of Rule 60(b) motions as subject to the reasonable-time requirement, cut against Petitioners’ effectively timeless regime; the better reconciliation is to read “reasonable time” as demanding heightened solicitude where the defect is truly fundamental (no notice/no arguable jurisdiction), not as authorizing atextual categorical immunity from timeliness. Under my methodology, creating an implied (b)(4) carveout because of constitutional rhetoric risks destabilizing finality and reliance interests without a clear textual hook, while the Rule’s text gives courts ample room to treat egregious voidness claims as timely even after substantial delay.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Alito press the best respondent point: Rule 60(c)(1) is facially categorical and Espinosa warns that (b)(4) is not a “license” to sleep on rights. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch explain, Espinosa’s “sleep on rights” concern is principally addressed by its narrow definition of “void” (no arguable jurisdictional basis/fundamental due-process defect), and once that threshold is met, continued enforcement is not mere finality but state-backed coercion without adjudicative authority. Reading “reasonable time” to categorically bar vacatur of a demonstrated nullity effectively allows procedure to entrench an ongoing constitutional deprivation—an outcome my pragmatic approach cannot accept, especially where default judgments predictably fall hardest on absent and vulnerable parties. I can accept the Roberts/Gorsuch limiting principle that delay may be probative of whether the claimed defect is truly Espinosa-level voidness (and may inform remedial tailoring), but not a freestanding timeliness bar once voidness is established.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Thomas’s “nullity” framing is powerful, but it mislocates what Rule 60(c)(1) does: as Justice Alito explains, it regulates access to the reopening remedy for motions “under Rule 60(b)” and does not purport to retroactively confer jurisdiction or “validate” anything. I also think Chief Justice Roberts’s proposal—treating delay as relevant only to whether the movant has shown Espinosa-level voidness—reads atextually into (c)(1) a carveout for (b)(4) that the Rule’s categorical language does not supply, especially in light of Kemp’s broad statement that Rule 60(b) motions are subject to the reasonable-time requirement. Espinosa’s admonition that (b)(4) is not a license to sleep on rights is difficult to reconcile with a regime where timeliness becomes categorically irrelevant whenever “void” is invoked; the better, coherent reading is that “reasonable time” applies but is calibrated to the nature of the defect (so truly jurisdictionless defaults will ordinarily satisfy it). I therefore remain with Respondent.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Kagan press the strongest point: Rule 60(c)(1) says motions “under Rule 60(b)” must be made within a reasonable time, and Kemp contains broad language along those lines. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas explain, that reading skips the antecedent question Espinosa foregrounds—whether the judgment is truly “void,” i.e., entered with no even arguable basis for personal jurisdiction or with a fundamental due-process failure; if so, the court lacked adjudicative authority ab initio and a timing rule cannot be used to keep enforcing what the law treats as a nullity. Espinosa’s “no license to sleep on rights” admonition is best understood as narrowing the category of “void,” not as authorizing courts to deny vacatur once voidness is established; delay may bear on whether the defect is actually Espinosa-level voidness (as Roberts suggests), but it cannot by itself supply power to maintain an ultra vires judgment. Kemp’s general statement cannot silently transform Rule 60(c)(1) into a validating mechanism for jurisdictional nullities without contradicting the traditional meaning of “void” and the constitutional limits it reflects.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas press the strongest point: a judgment entered without personal jurisdiction is a due-process nullity that time cannot “cure.” But that framing, as Justice Kagan explains, miscasts Rule 60(c)(1): enforcing a “reasonable time” limit regulates the availability of the reopening remedy under Rule 60(b), it does not retroactively confer jurisdiction or declare the underlying judgment valid. Espinosa’s admonition that (b)(4) is not a license to sleep on rights, together with Kemp’s broad instruction that Rule 60(b) motions are generally subject to Rule 60(c)(1), counsels against creating an atextual categorical exemption for (b)(4) even in personal-jurisdiction cases; the better course is to apply “reasonable time” with heightened sensitivity to truly Espinosa-level voidness without eliminating the timeliness requirement altogether. On an institutionalist view, petitioners’ approach risks destabilizing final judgments and reliance interests without sufficient textual warrant in the Rules we are bound to apply.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Thomas make the most powerful structural point: a judgment entered without personal jurisdiction is a nullity, and time cannot supply adjudicative authority the court never had. But that objection still does not overcome the Rules’ operative text: Rule 60(c)(1) categorically provides that motions “under Rule 60(b)”—including (b)(4)—“must be made within a reasonable time,” and as Justice Kagan stresses, enforcing that limit regulates the availability of reopening rather than retroactively ‘validating’ jurisdiction. Espinosa’s statement that (b)(4) is not a “license … to sleep on their rights,” together with Kemp’s broad treatment of the reasonable-time requirement for Rule 60(b) motions, undercuts petitioners’ proposed atextual carveout; the better reconciliation is to apply “reasonable time” with heightened sensitivity when the asserted defect is truly Espinosa-level voidness. I am therefore not persuaded by Justice Gorsuch’s proposal to make timeliness relevant only to diagnosing voidness and never to the remedy, because that effectively reads (c)(1)’s mandatory timing command out of the (b)(4) context without textual warrant.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Alito’s strongest point remains the categorical text of Rule 60(c)(1) and Kemp’s broad language that “all” Rule 60(b) motions must be brought within a reasonable time; I accept that atextual carveouts are disfavored. But Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch persuasively identify the antecedent constraint Espinosa imposes: if the judgment is truly void (no arguable basis for personal jurisdiction in a default posture), continued enforcement is beyond adjudicative authority, and a timing rule cannot do the constitutional work of making that deprivation lawful. Under my pragmatic, fairness-focused approach, delay can properly be used—as Roberts suggests—to test whether the movant is really presenting an Espinosa-level voidness claim rather than a forfeitable error, but once voidness is established, denying vacatur solely for timeliness entrenches a procedurally defective judgment against a non-appearing party in a way the Rules should not be read to require. Kemp’s general statement does not directly confront this specific (b)(4) nullity problem, and I would not extend it to authorize enforcement of a demonstrated due-process nullity.

John Roberts.reasoning: A default judgment entered without personal jurisdiction violates due process and is void; Rule 60(b)(4) exists to ensure courts do not give continuing effect to judgments issued without lawful authority. Although Rule 60(c)(1) states Rule 60(b) motions must be brought within a “reasonable time,” our cases treat (b)(4) relief as uniquely constrained to truly void judgments and not a discretionary, equitable reopening—making a rigid timeliness bar difficult to square with the concept of voidness. Espinosa explains that Rule 60(b)(4) relief is reserved for the exceptional case where there is not even an arguable basis for jurisdiction, and where that showing is made (as with a lack of personal jurisdiction in a default setting), finality interests cannot validate what due process forbids. A narrow holding can recognize that unreasonable delay may matter only insofar as it bears on whether the judgment is truly void (or on other non-(b)(4) avenues), but cannot by itself render a void judgment effectively immune from attack.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of Rule 60(b)(4) targets judgments that are “void,” and a default judgment entered without personal jurisdiction violates due process and is therefore a legal nullity that a court lacks authority to enforce. Although Rule 60(c)(1) generally says Rule 60(b) motions must be brought “within a reasonable time,” that language cannot be read to validate an ultra vires judgment or to confer jurisdiction by lapse of time; due process limits on personal jurisdiction forbid treating such a judgment as final. Espinosa recognizes that Rule 60(b)(4) relief is reserved for exceptional cases where the rendering court lacked even an arguable jurisdictional basis, and World-Wide Volkswagen underscores that a judgment rendered in violation of due process is void and not entitled to recognition. Any contrary implication in Kemp’s general statement about “all” Rule 60(b) motions yields where the judgment is void for want of personal jurisdiction, because there is nothing lawfully adjudicated to which finality can attach.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of Rule 60(c)(1) is categorical: motions “under Rule 60(b)”—including Rule 60(b)(4)—“must be made within a reasonable time,” and courts should not carve out an atextual exception for voidness claims. This Court’s cases caution against treating Rule 60(b)(4) as an open-ended license to upset final judgments after strategic delay; Espinosa specifically warned that Rule 60(b)(4) “does not provide a license for litigants to sleep on their rights,” and it narrowed “void” to exceptional jurisdictional or due-process defects rather than mere legal error. Reading Rule 60(c)(1) to apply to (b)(4) also best serves finality and practical consequences—especially in settings like a largely administered bankruptcy estate—while still permitting relief where a truly void judgment is promptly challenged. Kemp’s statement that all Rule 60(b) motions are subject to the “reasonable time” requirement reinforces the straightforward textual reading.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: A default judgment entered without personal jurisdiction violates due process and is void, not merely voidable, so Rule 60(b)(4) relief should remain available once voidness is shown and should not be cut off by Rule 60(c)(1)’s general “reasonable time” language. Espinosa teaches that Rule 60(b)(4) is reserved for the exceptional case where the rendering court lacked even an arguable basis for jurisdiction, and a judgment rendered in violation of due process is not entitled to legal effect—finality cannot cure a constitutional defect. Reading Rule 60(c)(1) to time-bar a true (b)(4) motion would allow an ultra vires judgment to become effectively valid through delay, a particularly unfair result in default settings where the defendant never appeared. Practical concerns about disruption can be addressed through careful application of the narrow Espinosa definition of “void” and through equitable management of remedies, but not by denying vacatur of a constitutionally void judgment.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Rule 60(c)(1) states categorically that a motion "under Rule 60(b)" must be made "within a reasonable time," and the most natural reading is that this timing rule applies to (b)(4) alongside the other subsections. Espinosa confirms that Rule 60(b)(4) is not a free-floating license to upset final judgments after sleeping on one’s rights—relief is reserved for the exceptional case, and parties can forfeit service-related objections through inaction even when they invoke voidness. That approach preserves due-process limits on personal jurisdiction while still giving effect to Rule 60(c)(1)’s workability and finality concerns, particularly where late disruption would prejudice third parties (e.g., an administered bankruptcy estate). Kemp’s statement that all Rule 60(b) motions are subject to the reasonable-time requirement reinforces that textual, administrable reading.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Rule 60(c)(1) says Rule 60(b) motions must be brought “within a reasonable time,” but Rule 60(b)(4) is triggered only when the “judgment is void”—and a judgment entered without personal jurisdiction is a due-process nullity, not merely an error that can be cured by delay. Espinosa teaches that voidness under Rule 60(b)(4) is reserved for exceptional cases involving certain jurisdictional defects or due-process violations, and when that standard is met the court has no discretion to leave the judgment in place; it follows that a “reasonable time” limit cannot operate to give continuing legal effect to a judgment rendered without power over the defendant. Reading Rule 60(c)(1) to bar relief here would effectively allow an ultra vires default judgment to become valid through passage of time, contrary to the Constitution’s due-process limits on personal jurisdiction and the original understanding that a void judgment is no judgment at all. Kemp’s general statement about timing cannot override the specific character of (b)(4) relief for void judgments, especially where the defendant never appeared and thus never consented to jurisdiction.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Rule 60(c)(1) states categorically that a motion under Rule 60(b) "must be made within a reasonable time," and that timing rule by its terms applies to (b)(4) as well as other subsections. Our cases emphasize that Rule 60(b)(4) relief is reserved for the exceptional case—when the rendering court lacked even an arguable basis for jurisdiction—which reflects a strong finality/legitimacy interest in not reopening long-settled judgments absent truly fundamental defects. See United Student Aid Funds, Inc. v. Espinosa, 559 U.S. 260, 271 (2010). Consistent with Kemp’s recognition that Rule 60(b) motions are generally subject to the “reasonable time” requirement, and given practical workability concerns (especially where third parties and reliance interests have accrued, as in a substantially administered bankruptcy estate), I would hold that (b)(4) motions remain subject to Rule 60(c)(1), with “reasonable time” applied in a way that accounts for the nature of a voidness claim and the equities of delay.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Rule 60(c)(1) states without qualification that a motion "under Rule 60(b)" must be made "within a reasonable time," and Rule 60(b)(4) is a subset of Rule 60(b); the most natural textual reading therefore applies the timing requirement to void-judgment motions as well. Espinosa confirms that Rule 60(b)(4) is not a limitless backdoor for late challenges, cautioning that it "does not provide a license for litigants to sleep on their rights" and recognizing forfeiture through inaction even when voidness is alleged. While due process limits on personal jurisdiction are serious, the Rule’s structure accommodates that concern by reserving (b)(4) relief for exceptional cases lacking even an arguable jurisdictional basis (Espinosa) while still allowing courts to police unreasonable delay under Rule 60(c)(1). Kemp’s statement that all Rule 60(b) motions must be filed within a reasonable time reinforces this plain-text and precedent-consistent interpretation.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: A default judgment entered without personal jurisdiction violates Due Process and is void, meaning the court lacked lawful power to bind the defendant in the first place; Rule 60(b)(4) exists to correct that foundational defect. Although Rule 60(c)(1) states that Rule 60(b) motions must be brought “within a reasonable time,” Espinosa teaches that voidness is reserved for the exceptional case where the rendering court lacked even an arguable basis for jurisdiction, and in that circumstance finality interests cannot convert an ultra vires judgment into a valid one. Reading Rule 60(c)(1) to categorically bar (b)(4) relief would, in practice, entrench procedurally unfair default judgments against absent defendants—precisely where the risk of unnoticed or unlitigated jurisdictional defects is highest—undermining the legitimacy of the process. Kemp’s general statement about “all Rule 60(b) motions” being subject to a reasonable-time requirement does not, in my view, override the constitutional imperative and the historic understanding that a truly void judgment must be set aside once voidness is established.
